title: Federal Reserve Set to Decide Rates as Warsh Faces First Major Inflation Test
summary: The Federal Reserve announces its interest rate decision on July 29, with markets overwhelmingly expecting a fifth straight hold at 3.50%-3.75%, though rising oil prices have fueled bets on a possible hike later in 2026.
description: The Federal Open Market Committee concludes its two-day meeting on July 29, with its interest rate decision due at 2 p.m. Eastern time, followed by a press conference led by Chair Kevin Warsh. Economists polled by major data providers overwhelmingly expect the central bank to leave its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.50% to 3.75%, which would mark the fifth consecutive meeting without a move. This meeting does not include an updated set of economic projections or a dot plot, so investors will focus on any changes to the policy statement and on Warsh's tone. The stakes are elevated because oil prices have climbed sharply during July amid renewed conflict between the United States and Iran, threatening to keep headline inflation hot and prompting traders to increase wagers on a rate increase later in the year. Adding to the uncertainty, Warsh has signaled a preference for less forward guidance than his predecessor, meaning markets may glean fewer clues about the path ahead. At the June meeting, officials were split, with half projecting a hike by year-end and half expecting no change.
image_alt: US Federal Reserve building representing the interest rate decision (illustrative)
key_points: The Fed's rate decision is due at 2 p.m. ET on July 29, followed by a Warsh press conference.
Markets overwhelmingly expect a fifth straight hold at 3.50%-3.75%.
This meeting has no updated projections or dot plot, so the statement and tone are key.
Rising oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict have lifted bets on a hike later in 2026.
why_it_matters: The Fed's decision and tone shape borrowing costs on mortgages, credit cards and business loans, and set the direction for markets and savings rates through the rest of 2026.

title: India's Sensex Jumps Over 650 Points as IT Stocks Lead a Broad Rally
summary: Indian benchmark indices rose sharply on July 29, with the Sensex climbing more than 650 points and the Nifty moving above 24,150, led by technology heavyweights and supported by foreign and domestic buying.
description: Indian equities extended their recovery on July 29, with the BSE Sensex surging more than 650 points in early trade and the NSE Nifty 50 climbing above the 24,150 mark. Technology shares led the advance, with Infosys jumping nearly 4% to top the Sensex gainers, alongside strength in L&T, TCS, Hindustan Unilever and Tech Mahindra. Power Grid, IndiGo, Asian Paints, Maruti and Titan were among the laggards. Market breadth was firmly positive, with advancing stocks outnumbering decliners by a wide margin on the National Stock Exchange. The rally built on a rebound earlier in the week after benchmark indices snapped a five-session losing streak, helped by easing geopolitical tensions in West Asia, a sharp fall in crude oil prices and caution ahead of the US Federal Reserve's policy decision. Foreign institutional investors turned net buyers, purchasing shares worth about Rs 755 crore in the prior session, while domestic institutions bought roughly Rs 1,664 crore. Investors are now watching the Fed outcome and ongoing quarterly corporate earnings for direction, with volatility expected to stay elevated around the monthly derivatives expiry.
image_alt: Stock market trading screen representing Indian equities rally (illustrative)
key_points: The Sensex rose more than 650 points and the Nifty climbed above 24,150 on July 29.
IT heavyweights led gains, with Infosys jumping nearly 4% in early trade.
Foreign investors turned net buyers, adding to domestic institutional buying.
Investors are watching the US Fed decision and quarterly earnings for cues.
why_it_matters: Equity market moves affect the savings and retirement portfolios of millions of Indian investors, and reflect sentiment around global rates, oil prices and corporate earnings.

title: Australian Inflation Cools More Than Expected, Easing Pressure on the RBA
summary: Australia's consumer prices rose less than forecast in the second quarter and in June, softening the case for a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and pushing the Australian dollar lower ahead of the August policy meeting.
description: Australia's inflation eased more than economists expected in the second quarter, offering relief to the Reserve Bank of Australia ahead of its August policy meeting. Official figures released on July 29 showed the consumer price index rose 4.0% in the June quarter from a year earlier, below the 4.1% forecast and down from 4.1% in the prior quarter. On a quarterly basis, prices increased 0.6%, a sharp slowdown from 1.4% in the March quarter. The closely watched trimmed mean measure of core inflation rose 3.6% year on year, down from 3.7% and below expectations. Separate monthly data showed headline inflation cooled to 3.8% in the year to June from 4.0% in May, with housing, food and recreation the largest contributors. The softer readings prompted several analysts to abandon their forecasts for further rate increases this year, and markets rapidly priced out the chance of a hike at the August meeting. The Australian dollar slipped following the data. The RBA's cash rate currently stands at 4.35%, and Governor Michele Bullock had reiterated the day before that policymakers remained ready to tighten further if inflation proved persistent.
image_alt: Australian currency and shopping basket representing inflation data (illustrative)
key_points: Australia's Q2 CPI rose 4.0% year on year, below the 4.1% forecast.
Core trimmed mean inflation eased to 3.6%, undershooting expectations.
Monthly headline inflation cooled to 3.8% in June from 4.0% in May.
Markets priced out an August RBA rate hike, and the Australian dollar fell.
why_it_matters: Cooler inflation lowers the risk of higher borrowing costs for Australian households and businesses, easing pressure on mortgage holders and shaping the RBA's next move.

title: Bank of Japan Expected to Hold at 1% as Yen Sinks Near a 40-Year Low
summary: The Bank of Japan is widely expected to keep its benchmark rate at 1% at its meeting ending July 31, with attention on an upgraded growth outlook and Governor Ueda's guidance as the yen trades near a four-decade low.
description: The Bank of Japan is widely expected to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 1% when its two-day policy meeting concludes on July 31, keeping borrowing costs at their highest since the mid-1990s. Investors are focused less on the rate itself than on the quarterly Outlook Report published alongside the decision and on the language Governor Kazuo Ueda uses at his afternoon press conference. Reports suggest the central bank may upgrade its growth forecast for the current fiscal year to around 0.8% from the 0.5% projected in April, while modestly trimming its inflation projection. The stakes are heightened by the yen, which has slid to its weakest level against the US dollar in roughly 40 years, trading near 163 to the dollar. That weakness raises import costs and complicates Ueda's messaging, as markets look for clues on whether the next rate increase could come in October or December. The BoJ has been gradually normalising policy after decades of ultra-low rates, and officials have signalled a continued tightening bias, though they remain wary of global risks including the conflict in the Middle East.
image_alt: Japanese yen banknotes representing central bank policy (illustrative)
key_points: The BoJ is expected to hold its rate at 1% at its meeting ending July 31.
The quarterly Outlook Report may upgrade fiscal 2026 growth to around 0.8%.
The yen has fallen to its weakest against the dollar in roughly 40 years.
Markets are watching Ueda's guidance on whether the next hike lands in October or December.
why_it_matters: The BoJ's stance and the weak yen influence global currency and bond markets, import costs for Japanese consumers, and international investment flows.

title: Bank of England Poised to Hold Rates at 3.75% Amid Sticky Services Inflation
summary: The Bank of England is expected to keep its base rate at 3.75% on July 30 alongside a new Monetary Policy Report, even as markets bet that stubborn services inflation could push rates higher over the coming year.
description: The Bank of England is widely expected to hold its base rate at 3.75% when its Monetary Policy Committee announces its decision at noon London time on July 30, accompanied by a fresh quarterly Monetary Policy Report and a press conference led by the Governor. Financial markets have all but ruled out a move at this meeting, with market-implied probabilities of no change running above 90%. Yet the same market pricing suggests the Bank Rate could head higher over the year ahead, reflecting concern about persistent price pressures. UK consumer price inflation stood at 2.8% in May, but services inflation rose to 3.7%, keeping policymakers cautious. The June meeting produced a 7-2 vote to hold, with two members preferring a hike to 4.00%, one more hawkish dissent than in April. The rebound in oil prices tied to renewed conflict in the Middle East has added to inflation risks and prompted some traders to bring forward expectations of rate rises. For borrowers, fixed mortgage pricing moves on swap rates rather than the Bank Rate directly, and two-year swaps have climbed in recent weeks, even as some lenders trimmed selected fixed deals.
image_alt: Row of UK houses representing mortgage and interest rate decisions (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of England is expected to hold its base rate at 3.75% on July 30.
A new Monetary Policy Report and press conference accompany the decision.
UK inflation was 2.8% in May, but services inflation rose to 3.7%.
Two-year swap rates have climbed, keeping upward pressure on fixed mortgage pricing.
why_it_matters: The Bank's decision and forecasts influence UK mortgage costs, savings rates and the pound, shaping household finances as borrowers weigh whether to fix now or wait.

title: Bank of Canada to Publish Deliberations Behind Its Latest Rate Hold
summary: The Bank of Canada releases the summary of deliberations on July 29 explaining its July 15 decision to hold rates at 2.25%, offering insight into how policymakers weighed a fragile recovery against inflation risks.
description: The Bank of Canada is set to publish, on July 29, the summary of deliberations behind its July 15 decision to keep its benchmark overnight rate unchanged at 2.25%, a sixth consecutive hold. The document, released in the afternoon Eastern time, offers a window into how the Governing Council weighed competing risks. At its July meeting, the central bank said Canada's economy had been weak but was showing signs of improvement, with growth expected to pick up and inflation projected to ease back toward 2%. Policymakers noted that economic growth appeared to have resumed after stalling over the past year, while the labour market remained soft, with unemployment at 6.5% in June. The Bank flagged two central risks to the outlook: the evolution of Canada's trade relationship with the United States, now subject to annual reviews, and the war in the Middle East, which has pushed up energy prices and fed cost pressures through supply chains. CPI inflation rose to 3.2% in May on higher gasoline costs, and the Bank expects it to ease in the second half of 2026. The next rate decision is scheduled for September 2.
image_alt: Central bank building representing monetary policy deliberations (illustrative)
key_points: The Bank of Canada publishes its summary of deliberations on July 29.
It explains the July 15 decision to hold the overnight rate at 2.25%, a sixth straight hold.
Policymakers cited US trade reviews and the Middle East war as the main risks.
CPI inflation was 3.2% in May and is expected to ease later in 2026.
why_it_matters: The deliberations reveal how close the central bank is to changing course, which affects mortgage and loan costs for Canadian households and the outlook for the loonie.

title: BNP Paribas Q2 Profit Jumps 33% and Hits Capital Target 18 Months Early
summary: France's largest bank reported its strongest quarterly revenue growth in a decade, with second-quarter net profit up about a third and its core capital ratio reaching a 13% target well ahead of schedule.
description: BNP Paribas, France's largest bank, reported second-quarter 2026 results showing its fastest revenue growth in a decade, with group revenue up 12% year on year and net profit climbing roughly a third to around 3 billion euros. The jump was amplified by an 858 million euro capital gain tied to a transaction restructuring its insurance partnership, though even excluding that one-off, adjusted earnings per share grew strongly. Crucially, the bank's Common Equity Tier 1 ratio, a key measure of financial strength, reached its 13% target a full 18 months ahead of the end-2027 goal. Management said the milestone paves the way for accelerated shareholder distributions, with the chief financial officer suggesting a payout ratio of 70% or more could be realistic from 2027, potentially including a special buyback. The results were broad-based: corporate and investment banking revenue rose 13%, led by record equities trading, while retail operations in France and Belgium recovered. Integration costs from the AXA Investment Managers acquisition and weakness at auto-leasing subsidiary Arval weighed on expenses, and the bank added provisions citing geopolitical concerns. BNP Paribas reaffirmed its 2026 and 2028 financial targets.
image_alt: Bank headquarters representing French banking earnings (illustrative)
key_points: BNP Paribas Q2 revenue rose 12%, its strongest in a decade, with net profit up about 33%.
Results were boosted by an 858 million euro gain from an insurance partnership restructuring.
Its CET1 capital ratio reached the 13% target 18 months ahead of schedule.
Management signalled larger shareholder payouts, potentially from 2027.
why_it_matters: As a systemically important European lender, BNP Paribas's strength signals resilience in the region's banking sector and points to bigger returns for shareholders.

title: Eurozone Inflation Eases to 2.8% as ECB Weighs Whether to Pause
summary: Euro area annual inflation slowed to 2.8% in June from 3.2% in May, the first decline since prices began accelerating early in the year, with Germany at 2.4% and France at 2.0% as the ECB considers its next step.
description: Euro area annual inflation eased to 2.8% in June from 3.2% in May, according to final figures from the European Union's statistics office, marking the first decline since prices began accelerating at the start of the year after the conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy supplies. While inflation remains above the European Central Bank's 2% target, the details of the release leaned toward a pause in rate rises. Core inflation, which strips out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, slowed to 2.4% from 2.6%, energy inflation cooled to 8.5% from 10.8%, and services inflation eased to 3.2% from 3.5%, with headline rates falling in the majority of member states. Among the bloc's largest economies, Germany stood at 2.4%, France at 2.0%, Italy at 3.0% and Spain at 3.6%. The moderation follows the ECB's decision at its June meeting to raise its deposit rate by a quarter point to 2.25%, its first increase in nearly three years, as policymakers responded to the energy-driven price surge. The cooler June reading gives the Governing Council room to assess whether that move should be followed by further tightening or a period of steady policy.
image_alt: Euro currency symbol representing eurozone inflation (illustrative)
key_points: Euro area inflation eased to 2.8% in June from 3.2% in May.
Core inflation slowed to 2.4%, and energy inflation cooled to 8.5%.
Germany stood at 2.4% and France at 2.0% among the big economies.
The data follows the ECB's June rate hike to a 2.25% deposit rate.
why_it_matters: Cooling eurozone inflation affects the ECB's rate path, which shapes borrowing costs, savings and mortgage rates for households and businesses across the currency bloc.

title: Dubai's DIFC Posts Record First-Half Growth Despite Regional Conflict
summary: The Dubai International Financial Centre reported record first-half performance in 2026, adding companies, jobs and assets under management even as conflict in the region weighed on the broader outlook.
description: The Dubai International Financial Centre, one of the Middle East's leading financial hubs, reported record first-half performance in 2026, underscoring the emirate's resilience as a magnet for global finance despite heightened regional tensions. The centre continued to attract new firms across banking, asset management, insurance and fintech, expanding its base of registered companies and creating jobs, while assets managed from the district grew. The results follow a record year in 2025 in which the DIFC added its largest-ever number of companies, and they come even as conflict between the United States and Iran has clouded the regional business environment and disrupted some flights and shipping. Officials attribute the continued growth to the UAE's political stability, business-friendly regulation, strong legal framework and its positioning as a bridge between East and West for capital flows. The performance reinforces the UAE's broader ambition to deepen its role in global financial services, wealth management and Islamic finance. For international banks, insurers and investment firms, the centre's expansion signals sustained demand to establish or grow a regional presence in Dubai, supporting the emirate's diversification away from oil.
image_alt: Dubai skyline representing the DIFC financial hub (illustrative)
key_points: The DIFC reported record first-half 2026 performance across companies, jobs and assets.
Growth continued despite regional conflict between the US and Iran.
The results follow a record 2025 for new company registrations.
Officials credit stability, regulation and Dubai's East-West positioning.
why_it_matters: The centre's growth reinforces Dubai's status as a global finance hub, drawing banks, insurers and investment firms and supporting the UAE's economic diversification.

title: UAE Fintech e& Money Wins Finance Licence to Offer Loans Through Its App
summary: The UAE central bank has granted e& money a finance company licence, allowing millions of users of the telecom-backed app to access credit and loan products directly through their phones.
description: The Central Bank of the UAE has granted a Finance Company Licence to e& money, the fintech arm linked to telecom group e&, enabling it to offer lending and credit products directly through its mobile app. The approval gives the platform's roughly two million users access to new borrowing options, expanding the range of digital financial services available on a single app that already handles payments and money transfers. The move reflects the UAE's broader push to build a cashless, digitally driven economy and to widen financial inclusion by bringing regulated credit to consumers through convenient mobile channels. By securing a formal licence, e& money comes under the central bank's supervisory framework, which sets standards for lending practices, consumer protection and risk management. For users, embedding loans within a familiar app can simplify access to credit, though it also raises the importance of responsible lending safeguards and clear terms. The licence is part of a wave of fintech activity in the Gulf, where regulators are balancing innovation with oversight as banks, telecom-backed platforms and startups compete to offer embedded finance. The development positions e& money to deepen its role in everyday consumer finance across the Emirates.
image_alt: Person using a mobile finance app representing digital lending (illustrative)
key_points: The UAE central bank granted e& money a Finance Company Licence.
Around two million app users gain access to new credit and loan options.
The licence brings the platform under central bank supervision.
It supports the UAE's push toward a cashless, financially inclusive economy.
why_it_matters: Embedding regulated lending in a widely used app expands access to credit for UAE consumers while placing digital lenders under central bank oversight for consumer protection.

title: US Stocks Wobble as Chip Selloff Tests Nerves Before Fed Decision
summary: US equities were mixed heading into the Federal Reserve decision, with the Dow holding up while the Nasdaq struggled through a bout of selling in semiconductor stocks amid stretched valuations.
description: US stocks turned choppy ahead of the Federal Reserve's July 29 policy decision, with strength in the Dow Jones Industrial Average offset by weakness in technology as a selloff swept through semiconductor shares. The Dow jumped hundreds of points in one recent session even as the Nasdaq Composite struggled, reflecting a rotation away from the chipmakers that had powered much of the market's advance this year. The pullback in semiconductors highlighted investor sensitivity to stretched valuations after a strong first half, in which major indexes repeatedly set records on optimism about artificial intelligence spending and resilient corporate earnings. With the Fed widely expected to hold rates steady but oil prices climbing on renewed Middle East conflict, traders are wary of any signal that inflation could delay rate relief. The absence of updated economic projections at this meeting leaves markets to parse the policy statement and Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference for direction. Beyond the Fed, investors are bracing for a dense stretch of data, including a first read on second-quarter economic growth and the central bank's preferred inflation gauge, along with a heavy slate of corporate earnings, all of which could drive sharp moves in the days ahead.
image_alt: Semiconductor chip representing a technology stock selloff (illustrative)
key_points: US stocks were mixed before the Fed decision, with the Dow up and the Nasdaq lagging.
A selloff in semiconductor shares tested nerves after a record-setting first half.
Stretched valuations left the market sensitive to any hawkish signal.
A dense run of GDP, inflation data and earnings looms in the days ahead.
why_it_matters: Swings in the biggest US stocks affect retirement and investment portfolios worldwide, and the Fed's tone could set the market's direction into the second half of 2026.

title: Demand for War-Risk Insurance Climbs in the UAE as Regional Tensions Persist
summary: Businesses in the UAE are increasingly seeking war-risk and political-violence insurance as renewed conflict in the region raises concerns about shipping, aviation and property exposures.
description: Demand for war-risk and political-violence insurance is rising in the UAE as renewed conflict in the region prompts businesses to reassess their exposures. Companies involved in shipping, aviation, logistics and property are increasingly seeking specialised cover that standard commercial policies typically exclude, as escalations between the United States and Iran raise the risk of disruption to trade routes and assets. War-risk insurance protects against losses arising from armed conflict, and its cost and availability tend to move sharply with geopolitical developments, particularly for vessels transiting sensitive waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Insurers and brokers in the Gulf have reported greater inquiries and, in some cases, higher premiums as underwriters price in elevated uncertainty. The trend underscores how regional instability feeds directly into the cost of doing business, from freight and energy shipments to airline operations and large construction projects. For the UAE, a major trade and re-export hub, the availability and affordability of such cover is important to keeping commerce flowing. Risk managers are being urged to review policy wordings closely, since exclusions, geographic limits and waiting periods can significantly affect whether a claim is paid.
image_alt: Cargo ships at port representing war-risk shipping insurance (illustrative)
key_points: War-risk and political-violence insurance demand is rising in the UAE.
Shipping, aviation and property firms are most affected by regional conflict.
Premiums can spike for vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea.
Risk managers are urged to review exclusions and policy limits carefully.
why_it_matters: Rising war-risk premiums increase the cost of trade, shipping and aviation for UAE businesses, feeding into prices and highlighting how geopolitics affects everyday commerce.

title: RBI Rolls Out Ambitious FY27 Agenda With e-Kuber 3.0 and Tech Upgrades
summary: The Reserve Bank of India has set out a wide-ranging agenda for 2026-27, including a review of the RBI Act and a next-generation core banking system, e-Kuber 3.0, alongside a new alternative payment system.
description: The Reserve Bank of India has unveiled a comprehensive agenda for the 2026-27 financial year, signalling a significant push on technology and institutional modernisation. Among the headline initiatives is a plan to launch its next-generation core banking system, e-Kuber 3.0, along with an alternative payment system and a unified enterprise platform, upgrades intended to strengthen the resilience and efficiency of the country's financial infrastructure. The central bank also plans to review the RBI Act, the legislation that underpins its powers and mandate, as part of broader efforts to keep its framework aligned with a rapidly evolving financial system. The agenda comes as the RBI continues to manage a delicate balance between supporting credit growth and controlling inflation. Recent data showed banks raising the weighted average lending rate on fresh rupee loans, reflecting robust credit demand, even as the central bank works to improve the transmission of its policy rate to market lending rates. The RBI has kept its benchmark repo rate at 5.25% in recent meetings while maintaining a neutral stance, citing resilient domestic activity despite risks from the conflict in West Asia and an uneven monsoon. The technology roadmap underscores the bank's ambition to build faster, safer and more inclusive digital finance.
image_alt: Digital banking infrastructure representing RBI technology upgrades (illustrative)
key_points: The RBI has set out a broad technology and reform agenda for 2026-27.
Plans include the e-Kuber 3.0 core banking system and an alternative payment system.
The central bank intends to review the RBI Act.
The repo rate remains at 5.25% with a neutral stance amid global risks.
why_it_matters: Upgrades to India's core financial infrastructure aim to make payments and banking faster, safer and more inclusive for consumers and businesses across the country.

title: Trump Accounts Roll Out Across the US With $1,000 Seed for Newborns
summary: New tax-advantaged Trump Accounts for American children are now rolling out following their July 4 launch, offering a $1,000 government deposit for eligible newborns and room for family and employer contributions.
description: Trump Accounts, the new tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children created under the 2025 tax-and-spending law, are rolling out across the United States following their launch on July 4. The accounts function much like a traditional individual retirement account for minors, with the child as the legal owner and a parent or guardian managing the account until age 18. The federal government makes a one-time $1,000 contribution for children born from the start of 2025 through the end of 2028, once an account is opened. Beyond that seed, parents, relatives and others can contribute up to a combined $5,000 a year, with employers able to add up to $2,500 within that cap, and the government deposit and certain charitable gifts do not count toward the limit. Investments are restricted to low-cost US index funds, and withdrawals are generally barred before age 18. Families are weighing the accounts against established options such as 529 education plans and custodial accounts, each with different tax treatment and withdrawal rules. Financial advisers note that while the government seed money is a clear benefit, the accounts' long-term value will depend on contributions, investment returns and how the withdrawal rules are applied once children reach adulthood.
image_alt: Parent and child with a piggy bank representing children's savings accounts (illustrative)
key_points: Trump Accounts are rolling out after their July 4 launch.
Eligible children born 2025-2028 receive a one-time $1,000 government deposit.
Families can add up to a combined $5,000 a year, with employers up to $2,500 within the cap.
Advisers suggest weighing them against 529 plans and custodial accounts.
why_it_matters: The accounts give millions of American children a government-funded head start on investing, but families must compare them with other tax-advantaged savings options.

title: South Korean Stocks Near Records as Chip Rally Powers the Kospi
summary: South Korea's stock market has led regional gains in 2026, buoyed by a semiconductor and artificial intelligence boom, though the won has come under pressure and profit-taking has capped some of the advance.
description: South Korean equities have been among the strongest performers in Asia in 2026, with the benchmark Kospi index trading near record highs as a global boom in semiconductors and artificial intelligence supercharges demand for the country's memory chips and advanced components. Korean and Japanese shares have repeatedly led regional gains this year, drawing both domestic retail investors and foreign inflows into a market that had long traded at a discount to global peers. The rally has been underpinned by extraordinary export strength, with the country's semiconductor shipments surging as data-centre and AI investment accelerates worldwide. At the same time, the advance has not been one-directional: bouts of profit-taking have periodically pulled shares back, and the won has slipped against the dollar even as equities climbed, reflecting the pull of higher US yields and a firm greenback. Policymakers at the Bank of Korea have flagged financial stability risks, including rising household debt and leveraged stock investments, as more first-time investors pile into the market. For now, the combination of resilient earnings, an AI-driven export cycle and easing valuations has kept sentiment broadly positive, though investors remain alert to any cooling in the semiconductor upturn.
image_alt: Stock market chart representing the South Korean equity rally (illustrative)
key_points: The Kospi has traded near record highs in 2026 on a chip and AI boom.
Korean and Japanese shares have led regional gains this year.
The won has weakened against the dollar even as equities climbed.
The Bank of Korea has flagged risks from household debt and leveraged investing.
why_it_matters: South Korea is a bellwether for global tech demand, so its market strength reflects the scale of the AI cycle, while currency weakness and leverage pose risks for investors.
